stops.title: Welcome to the atlas
stops.text: Welcome to this atlas of sixteen papers on compressing video diffusion models. The thesis behind it takes LTX-2.3, a model that turns a text prompt into a video with sound, and makes it smaller and faster on an Intel CPU and an Intel Arc GPU without breaking its output. Each paper tab has a short intro, a guided tour, and a written guide for every figure and equation. With auto-continue on, everything plays in order. This tab lays the foundation.

stops.title: The whole pipeline
stops.text: First, the whole system. The prompt goes into Gemma 3, a twelve billion parameter text encoder that runs only once. Then comes the dual-stream diffusion transformer, with nineteen billion parameters for video and audio, which runs again and again, once or several times per denoising step. At the end, small decoders turn the result into frames and sound. The transformer is both the largest part and the most repeated one, so it is the first target.

stops.title: What smaller means
stops.text: So what do smaller and faster actually mean? Smaller means fewer bytes per weight. Memory is roughly the number of parameters times the bytes each one takes, so moving from sixteen-bit to four-bit weights shrinks the transformer about four times. Faster then follows in two ways: fewer bytes travel from memory at every step, or the number of steps goes down. Every setting in this project is measured on size, speed and quality together.

stops.title: How diffusion works
stops.text: Now to diffusion itself, and why the transformer runs so often. Diffusion builds a video by removing noise in many small steps. It starts from pure noise, and at each step the transformer looks at the noisy latent and the timestep, shown in gold, and predicts a move toward a clean result. The same network sees very different inputs early and late in the process. That is exactly why quantization papers for diffusion care about timesteps.

stops.title: Working in latent space
stops.text: But the transformer never touches raw pixels. A variational autoencoder, or VAE, first squeezes the video into a compact latent, and diffusion runs only on that latent. So the transformer sees thousands of tokens instead of millions of pixels, and the decoder expands the final latent back into frames only once, at the end. LTX-2 adds a second, one-dimensional audio VAE that works the same way for the soundtrack. Generate small, decode big.

stops.title: Guidance multiplies cost
stops.text: There is one more multiplier on cost. Classifier-free guidance runs the transformer twice, once with the prompt and once without, and pushes the result away from the prompt-free answer by a guidance scale. That is equation one just below, and it makes the video follow the text more closely. LTX-2 adds a third pass that drops the other modality. So a single denoising step can cost up to three full transformer calls.

stops.title: Linear layers are GEMMs
stops.text: Now to transformers, in five minutes. The basic unit is the linear layer. Each token is a row of numbers, and multiplying all tokens by a weight matrix at once is a general matrix multiply, or GEMM. The weights hold the model's knowledge and never change. The activations change with every prompt and every step. Weight-only compression, the main track of the thesis, shrinks the weights and leaves the activations alone.

stops.title: Attention grows quadratically
stops.text: Attention works differently. Each token makes a query, a key and a value, and comparing every query with every key gives a table of scores that grows with the number of tokens squared. Equation two below states it: attention cost grows with the square of the token count, while a linear layer grows only in proportion. A short LTX-Video clip already has about six thousand latent tokens. And since attention has no weights, weight compression does not shrink it.

stops.title: Inside a DiT block
stops.text: Put those pieces together and we get one diffusion transformer block, stacked many times. Tokens pass through self-attention, where they look at each other, cross-attention, where they look at the text and in LTX-2 also at the other stream, and a feed-forward network. Almost every box is built from linear layers. The timestep enters through the gold path, called AdaLN, which sets a scale, shift and gate in each block, so the same weights behave differently at each noise level.

stops.title: Floats and integers
stops.text: Now to numbers, and quantization from zero. A floating-point number splits its bits into a sign, an exponent that sets how big it is, and a mantissa that sets how precise it is. So a float carries its own scale. An integer is just an evenly spaced level, so eight-bit and four-bit integers need an extra scale factor to stand for a real value. LTX-2.3 ships in B F sixteen, and the compressed weights become integers plus scales.

stops.title: Memory at each precision
stops.text: This table puts numbers on that. At thirty-two bits, the nineteen billion parameter transformer needs seventy-six gigabytes. At sixteen bits, as released, it needs thirty-eight. Eight-bit weights halve that to nineteen, and four-bit weights with one scale per group of one hundred twenty-eight bring it to about nine point eight gigabytes. The equations below give the quick estimate, parameters times bytes, then define the scale, the zero-point, and the quantize and dequantize steps we are about to see in action.

stops.title: A worked INT4 example
stops.text: Here those equations are worked through. The weights span minus zero point six to zero point nine. With sixteen levels, the step is zero point one and the zero-point is six. The value zero point two three becomes level eight and comes back as zero point two, a small rounding error. But the magenta value one point three lies outside the range, is clipped, and returns as zero point nine. Stretching the range would make every step coarser instead.

stops.title: Who shares a scale
stops.text: That trade-off leads to a design choice: how many numbers share one scale. The fewer numbers per scale, the tighter the fit and the smaller the error, but more scales must be stored. Weights are usually scaled per output channel for eight bits, or per group of sixty-four or one hundred twenty-eight inputs for four bits. Activations change at every step, so papers often scale them per token on the fly, shown in gold.

stops.title: Reading WxAy names
stops.text: Papers name their schemes by the bits of weights and activations. W four A sixteen means four-bit weights and sixteen-bit activations. Weight-only schemes like that decompress the weights inside the kernel and compute in sixteen-bit, so they mainly save memory and memory traffic. Schemes such as W eight A eight or W four A four also quantize activations, which unlocks integer matrix units but exposes activation outliers. The core track of the thesis is weight-only.

stops.title: The outlier problem
stops.text: And here is the central difficulty. In large transformers, a few channels carry values far bigger than all the rest, shown in magenta. If one scale has to cover them, the step becomes huge, and ordinary values collapse onto one or two levels. Most quantization papers in this atlas are, at heart, different answers to this problem: smaller groups, moving outliers into the weights, rotating them away, or keeping them in higher precision.

stops.title: PTQ, QAT, mixed precision
stops.text: Three terms appear in almost every paper. Post-training quantization, or PTQ, needs only a trained model and a small calibration set, which for diffusion must cover many timesteps. Quantization-aware training, or QAT, retrains the model with rounding simulated, at a cost of days of GPU time. Mixed precision gives each layer its own bit width, keeping the few sensitive layers at higher precision. This project works in the post-training setting.

stops.title: Compute is close, data far
stops.text: Now to hardware, and why speed is not just a count of operations. A CPU has a few powerful cores with wide vector units. A GPU has many simpler cores plus matrix units, and usually its own fast memory. Each level of the memory hierarchy is faster but smaller than the one below. A thirty-eight gigabyte model cannot sit in any cache, so every denoising step streams the weights in from main memory.

stops.title: The roofline idea
stops.text: The roofline picture shows what that means for speed. An operation that does little arithmetic per byte it loads is memory-bound: bandwidth caps its speed, and shrinking the bytes, for example with four-bit weights, moves it up the slope. An operation that does a lot of arithmetic per byte is compute-bound, and weight-only compression then saves memory but little time. Where LTX-2.3's layers sit on the Intel CPU and Arc GPU must be measured, not assumed.

stops.title: Kernels and fusion
stops.text: How the work is packaged matters too. A kernel is one compiled routine that runs an operation on the chip. Running operations as separate kernels sends every intermediate result out to memory and back again. A fused kernel does several steps in one pass and keeps the data on the chip. FlashAttention is this idea applied to attention, and OpenVINO fuses many common patterns automatically when it compiles a model.

stops.title: Speed belongs to hardware
stops.text: Which leads to an important warning. Many papers report speed-ups from custom CUDA kernels on NVIDIA GPUs, using Tensor Cores, the NVIDIA matrix units that run certain low-precision formats much faster. Intel Arc GPUs have matching engines called XMX. But if a format has no fast kernel in OpenVINO, a method's accuracy gains may still carry over while its speed-up does not. A reported speed-up always belongs to its hardware.

stops.title: The software stack
stops.text: Now to the software stack this project uses: export, compress, compile, compare. Optimum Intel traces each part of the diffusers pipeline into OpenVINO's intermediate representation, a graph file plus a weight file. NNCF rewrites those weights as eight-bit or four-bit integers with scales. At load time, OpenVINO compiles the result for the CPU or GPU and picks its own kernels, so no custom kernel is written. Every setting is then compared with the PyTorch reference.

stops.title: Measuring quality
stops.text: How can anyone tell the model was not broken? That is the job of quality metrics. Paired metrics compare the compressed output with the full-precision output for the same prompt and seed, so they directly measure damage. Unpaired metrics score realism, text match or video properties on their own, and are used to compare different models. The thesis plan combines both: WWB similarity from OpenVINO's GenAI tools for paired checks, and a subset of VBench for video qualities.

stops.title: Speeding up without bits
stops.text: Quantization is not the only lever. There are four that stack. Quantization shortens each step. Step caching, as in DeepCache and TeaCache, reuses an earlier result when a cheap signal says the output barely changed. Distillation retrains the model to need fewer steps, which lies outside this project's scope. Efficient attention does the same math with less memory traffic. Caching needs no calibration and no custom kernels, which makes TeaCache the natural optional extra.

stops.title: Map of the papers
stops.text: Finally, the map of all sixteen papers. The language-model quantizers, GPTQ, SmoothQuant and AWQ, are the tools NNCF already implements. The diffusion papers adapt them to timesteps, video tokens and outliers. SmoothQuant-style scaling reappears in PTQ4DiT, ViDiT-Q and SVDQuant, and the Wan two point two paper combines SVDQuant with GPTQ. Indigo boxes are the papers the thesis uses directly, the others explain limits and alternatives, and the arrows mark only links the papers state.

stops.title: How the atlas works
stops.text: So how is the atlas meant to be used? Each paper tab opens with a two-minute intro on what that paper assumes, then a guided tour of its story in about five minutes, scrolling to each key figure. Every figure, equation and table has its own guide, a short spoken-style explanation. And every tab ends with a thesis box that says what the paper means in practice for OpenVINO and NNCF.

stops.title: Glossary and wrap-up
stops.text: The glossary collects every term from this primer, from activation and AdaLN to calibration data and compute-bound, for quick lookup at any point. To sum up: the transformer is the bottleneck, diffusion calls it many times, weight quantization shrinks its linear layers, outliers make that hard, and speed depends on memory and on the kernels the hardware actually has. Next comes the first paper, LTX-Video.
